headline: High-risk Cursor defaults can write, shell, and egress broadly; the paired cheatsheet is read-only, so main risks are prompt injection and cascading misuse rather than direct conflict.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Cursor can read workspace files, open buffers, clipboard, and use MCP, so attacker-controlled content can reach its agent loop. python-cheatsheet is documentation-only and read-only, so it is not an active injector, but if its text is copied into Cursor or opened in the workspace, instructions could be misread as commands.
conditions: IF python-cheatsheet content is pasted into Cursor chat or opened in a workspace file
IF Cursor parses file or clipboard content as instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Disable clipboard-based prompt ingestion in Cursor
Keep cheatsheet content in a separate read-only window
Use explicit delimiters around pasted reference text
Turn off MCP servers not needed for the task
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for imported text

B_data_leakage.rationale: Cursor touches source code, open files, and clipboard contents and can send data to model providers and MCP servers. python-cheatsheet touches no data classes and has no I/O surfaces, so it is not a leakage source; the risk is Cursor exfiltrating sensitive workspace content to third parties during normal use.
conditions: IF sensitive code or secrets are present in Cursor's workspace
IF Cursor routes those contents to external model providers or MCP servers
mitigations: Remove secrets from the workspace before use
Disable nonessential model-provider routing
Audit MCP server destinations
Use a separate non-sensitive workspace for reference material
requires-engineering: enforce data-loss-prevention filters

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Cursor has broad filesystem write and git modification capability, while python-cheatsheet has no write, network, or subprocess capabilities. There is no meaningful overlapping mutable resource, so direct capability conflict is limited to unusual manual workflows that copy edits from the cheatsheet into Cursor.
conditions: IF an operator manually transfers edits from python-cheatsheet into Cursor-managed files
IF both are pointed at the same git working tree through external tooling
mitigations: Avoid concurrent edits to the same repo
Use git status before committing
Keep the cheatsheet outside the writable workspace
Pause one agent while the other writes
requires-engineering: add file-lock coordination

D_cascading_error.rationale: Cursor can act on generated code and shell commands, so if it treats python-cheatsheet output as authoritative, mistakes can cascade into edits or commands. The cheatsheet is static reference material, not an action-taking agent, so the pathway is one-way but still plausible in default coding workflows.
conditions: IF Cursor uses cheatsheet text as authoritative guidance without verification
IF Cursor then applies that guidance to code edits or shell commands
mitigations: Verify snippets against official docs before acting
Require human review for generated commands
Use tests before applying edits
Keep reference material clearly labeled as non-authoritative
requires-engineering: add citation/verification gating

E_compliance.rationale: Cursor handles source code, open files, and clipboard contents and may send them to external providers, but the cheatsheet profile has no sensitive data classes or residency constraints. No specific compliance mismatch is evidenced between the pair, so only a small risk exists if regulated data is manually placed into Cursor.
conditions: IF regulated data is pasted into Cursor
IF external model-provider processing is disallowed for that data class
mitigations: Do not place regulated data in the workspace
Use local-only models for sensitive tasks
Review retention settings before use
Separate compliant and noncompliant projects
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls
